title: Who Gets a Seat at the Table
sum: On a Sabbath Jesus eats at the house of a leading Pharisee. A man with dropsy stands in front of him; Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether healing is allowed on the Sabbath, heals the man, and silences them with a question about a son or an ox fallen down a well (14:1–6). Watching the guests grab the top places, he tells them to take the last place and wait to be called up, for "everyone who raises himself up will be brought low" (14:7–11). He tells his host to invite people who cannot repay him: the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind (14:12–14).

When a guest says, "How blessed is whoever eats bread in the kingdom of God!", Jesus answers with the parable of the great supper. The invited guests all make excuses, so the angry host fills his house with the poor and disabled of the town, and then with whoever can be found on the country roads (14:15–24). On the road again, Jesus turns to the crowds following him: no one can be his disciple without putting him above family and life itself, carrying the cross, and saying goodbye to all possessions. Count the cost, as a builder or a king does, and do not be like salt that has gone flat (14:25–35).
readings: Read as table talk

Luke stages the chapter like a Greek symposium, a dinner where the guests discuss a question. Here the host and guests are taught by the one they are watching. Each scene turns on the table: who is healed at it, who sits where, who is invited, who refuses to come. Read this way, the chapter is about honor, and Jesus overturns the rules that decide it.
Read as a picture of the mission

The great supper follows the shape of Luke-Acts. The invited guests refuse; the poor and disabled of the town are brought in; then the slave goes out to the roads beyond. Many readers since the church fathers have seen here Israel's leaders refusing, the outcasts of Israel welcomed by Jesus, and the Gentiles brought in by the apostles (Acts 13:46).
Read as a call to count the cost

The chapter ends not at the table but on the road, with large crowds. Their enthusiasm is not enough. Read this way, the banquet and the cost belong together: the feast is free, and it costs everything, because to come to it means leaving the excuses of field, oxen and marriage behind.

views.H: Sabbath meals were the high point of the Jewish week, eaten at midday after the synagogue and cooked the day before. Greco-Roman dinners were arranged by rank, with the host and his most honored guests on the central couch, and invitations were part of a system of favors returned. The disabled and the destitute lived at the edges of town life, often by begging. Jesus' advice to invite them breaks both the Jewish purity concerns seen at Qumran and the Roman habit of feeding those who can repay.
views.C: Luke 14 gathers material from several sources. The Sabbath healing (14:1–6) and the advice on seating (14:7–14) are found only in Luke. The great supper has a parallel in Matthew 22:1–14 and another in the Gospel of Thomas 64; most scholars trace Luke and Matthew to a shared source (Q) that each reshaped, though some think Luke reworked Matthew. The sayings on hating family and carrying the cross (14:26–27) have parallels in Matthew 10:37–38, and the salt saying in Matthew 5:13 and Mark 9:50. The tower and the king (14:28–32) are Luke's alone.
views.L: Luke builds a chain of linked scenes on one setting. The word "invite" (καλέω) runs through the chapter (14:7–10, 12–13, 16–17, 24), and the guest list of the needy appears twice (14:13, 21), tying Jesus' advice to the host to the parable. The chapter moves from a table where people are watched (14:1) to a road where crowds follow (14:25), and from honor at a dinner to the cost of the cross.
views.J: Jesus is a guest in a Pharisee's house on the Sabbath, and the debate is an in-house Jewish argument about how to keep the Sabbath, which the Torah commands but does not define in detail. Jewish groups differed: the Qumran sect was stricter than the later rabbis. Proverbs 25:6–7 lies behind the advice on seating, and Isaiah 25's feast for all peoples behind the banquet. Jewish readers note that Luke's Pharisees invite Jesus and argue with him at table, which is how disputes among Jewish teachers were carried on.
views.T: The parable of the great supper was read in the Western church as an image of the Eucharist and of the church's mission, and its "compel them to come in" was, from Augustine onward, a proof-text for using force against heretics and schismatics, a use the churches now reject (see the card below). The sayings on hating family and renouncing possessions shaped monastic life: Basil the Great's rules for monks cite them as the pattern of renunciation.

deep.b:
Luke shows Jesus at table more than any other Gospel. He eats with tax collectors at Levi's house (5:29), with Simon the Pharisee (7:36), with five thousand in the wilderness (9:10–17), with Martha and Mary (10:38–42), with Pharisees again (11:37; 14:1), with Zacchaeus (19:5), with the Twelve at the Last Supper (22:14–38) and with two disciples at Emmaus, where he is known "in the breaking of the bread" (24:30–35). His enemies call him a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34).

Meals in Luke show who belongs. They are where Jesus teaches about status (14:7–11), about whom to invite (14:12–14) and about the feast of the kingdom (13:29; 14:15–24; 22:16, 30). Willi Braun and others have compared chapter 14 to the Greek symposium, the literary form of a dinner with philosophical conversation (as in Plato's Symposium and Plutarch's Table Talk), in which the wise guest teaches the company. Acts continues the pattern in the believers' shared meals (Acts 2:46) and in Peter's eating with the Gentile Cornelius (Acts 10–11).

Matthew and Luke both tell of a host whose invited guests refuse to come, but the two stories differ at almost every point.

Luke 14:16–24Matthew 22:1–14
SettingA Pharisee's Sabbath meal, on the road to JerusalemThe temple courts, to the chief priests and Pharisees, in the last week
Host"Someone"A king, at his son's wedding
RefusalThree polite excusesIndifference; some guests kill the slaves
ResponseThe poor and disabled of the town, then people from the roadsThe king's army burns their city; then everyone from the roads, "evil and good"
EndingNone of the invited will taste the supperA guest without wedding clothes is thrown out

The Gospel of Thomas (saying 64) has a third version: a man's guests decline with four excuses about business, a house, a friend's wedding and a farm, and the saying ends, "Buyers and merchants will not enter the places of my Father." Most scholars think Matthew and Luke drew on a common source (Q) and shaped it for their purposes: Matthew toward judgment on Jerusalem's leaders, Luke toward the welcome of the poor. Others think Jesus told such a story more than once, or that Luke reworked Matthew. Thomas is usually dated later and thought to depend on the Synoptic tradition, though some scholars treat its form as independent.

deep.h: "Compel them to come in": a verse's long shadow
deep.b:
In the story the master's order is about urgent hospitality (see the note on 14:23). In history the verse, in its Latin form compelle intrare, became one of the best-known texts in Christian debates over force.

Augustine at first opposed using imperial power against the Donatists, the rival church in North Africa. He changed his mind after seeing whole towns return to the Catholic Church under the laws, and in his letters to Vincentius (Letter 93, AD 408) and to the official Boniface (Letter 185, about AD 417) he read the two sendings of the slave as two stages: invitation to those inside, compulsion for those outside. He insisted the aim was correction, not cruelty, and opposed the death penalty for Donatists. Later writers used his reading to defend far harsher measures against heretics, Jews and dissenters.

The Reformation did not settle the question at once. The Augsburg Confession says bishops are to exercise their office without human force, by the Word alone (article 28), and Luther wrote that heresy, a spiritual matter, cannot be held back by force (Temporal Authority, 1523); yet Lutheran princes enforced one confession in their lands for two centuries. Calvin defended the punishment of heresy, and the Westminster Confession gave the magistrate the duty to see that heresies were suppressed (23.3), a section American Presbyterians rewrote in 1788 to deny the state any power over matters of faith. The Anabaptists' Schleitheim Confession (1527) placed the sword "outside the perfection of Christ," and Anabaptists were persecuted by Catholic and Protestant rulers alike.

In 1686, the year after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and French Protestants were forced to convert, the Protestant philosopher Pierre Bayle published a Philosophical Commentary on these words. He argued that any reading of Scripture that commands cruelty must be a false reading. Baptists such as Thomas Helwys (1612) and Roger Williams had already argued for liberty of conscience, and the Second London Confession says that God alone is Lord of the conscience (21.2). Today the Catholic Church teaches that no one may be forced to embrace the faith (Dignitatis Humanae 10; Catechism 160), and no major church defends Augustine's use of the verse.

echoes: Proverbs 25:6–7; Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 22:4; Leviticus 21:17–23; Isaiah 25:6–9; Deuteronomy 20:5–7; Deuteronomy 24:5; Genesis 29:30–31; Esther 5:8; Esther 6:14; Matthew 22:1–14; Matthew 10:37–38; Matthew 5:13; Mark 9:49–50; Matthew 23:12; 6:6–11; 13:10–17; 18:14; 9:23; 9:57–62; 23:26; Acts 13:46

settings.what: The question about healing on the Sabbath
settings.to: the lawyers and Pharisees at a Sabbath meal in the house of a leading Pharisee
settings.when: as a man swollen with dropsy stood in front of him, with everyone watching
settings.why: The Sabbath command bound every Israelite household to rest from work (Exodus 20:8–11), but whether healing was "work" was argued among Jewish groups: stricter ones forbade even helping an animal out of a pit, while later rabbis let the saving of life override the Sabbath. Jesus asks the experts to rule first, and when they keep silent, he heals and then argues from what they themselves would do for a son or an ox. The point is not to abolish the Sabbath but to show that doing good belongs to it.
settings.readers: Luke's mostly Gentile readers saw Jesus keep the Sabbath inside Jewish debate, as a teacher of Israel, not as a rule-breaker; the Sabbath remained a live question for mixed churches (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16).

settings.what: The parable of the places at table
settings.to: the invited guests at the Pharisee's meal
settings.when: after he noticed them choosing the top places for themselves
settings.why: On the surface, practical advice from Proverbs 25:6–7 about avoiding public shame. Underneath, a parable about God's judgment: in the kingdom, those who push themselves forward will be put down, and those who take the low place will be called up. It confronts the guests' scramble for honor in front of the one they have been watching.
settings.readers: Luke's churches, where rich and poor met at the same table and status quarrels broke out (compare James 2:1–4; 1 Corinthians 11:17–22), heard it as a rule for their own gatherings.

settings.what: Advice to the host about whom to invite
settings.to: the leading Pharisee who had invited him
settings.when: at the same Sabbath meal
settings.why: To break the circle of invitations given to earn invitations back. Jesus tells his host to invite the poor and disabled, who cannot repay, and to look to God's repayment at the resurrection of the righteous, a hope a Pharisee shared. It turns hospitality from an investment into a gift.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers it described the shared meals of the church (Acts 2:44–46; 6:1) and the duty of better-off members to feed the poor.

settings.what: A guest's blessing on the kingdom's feast
settings.by: one of the guests at the table
settings.to: Jesus, before the whole company
settings.when: after Jesus spoke of repayment at the resurrection of the righteous
settings.why: A pious remark, perhaps meant to round off the conversation on a safe note: everyone at the table expects a place at God's banquet. Jesus' parable answers it by asking whether those who expect a seat will actually come.

settings.what: The parable of the great supper
settings.to: the guest who spoke, and the Pharisees, lawyers and guests at the meal
settings.when: at the Sabbath meal, after the guest's blessing
settings.why: To warn people who assume they belong at God's banquet that they may refuse the invitation when it comes, with polite excuses about land, livestock and marriage, while the poor and the outsiders whom they despise are brought in. The plural "I tell you" of 14:24 turns the parable directly on the listeners.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw in it their own history: Jesus' welcome of outcasts, the refusal of many in Israel, and the gathering of Gentiles from "the roads and the hedgerows."
views: A Pharisee's dinner, aimed at respectable people who take their place in the kingdom for granted; the newcomers are the poor and disabled.

In Matthew 22:1–14 a similar parable is told in the temple during Jesus' last week, to the chief priests and Pharisees, as a judgment on Jerusalem's leaders, with a burned city and a guest thrown out for lacking wedding clothes.
Thomas 64 aims a similar story at buyers and merchants, with no mention of the poor.

settings.what: The cost of being a disciple, with the twin parables of the tower and the king
settings.to: the large crowds walking along with him on the road to Jerusalem
settings.when: after leaving the Pharisee's house, as more and more people followed him
settings.why: To thin a crowd drawn by excitement. Jesus states his claims without softening them: loyalty to him above family and life, the cross, and parting with possessions. The tower and the king tell people to count the cost before they start, and the salt saying warns that a disciple who will not pay it is good for nothing.
settings.readers: Luke's readers included believers who had lost family ties and property for their faith (18:28–30; Acts 2:44–45; Hebrews 10:34). The chapter told them the loss had been foreseen, and was the price of a real discipleship.

title: Lost and Found
sum: Tax collectors and sinners crowd around to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes grumble: "This fellow takes sinners in, and he eats with them!" (15:1–2). Jesus answers with three stories. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to search for one that is lost, carries it home on his shoulders and calls his friends to celebrate. A woman lights a lamp and sweeps the house until she finds one lost silver coin, and calls her friends and neighbors to rejoice. Each time Jesus adds: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (15:3–10).

The third story is the longest. A younger son takes his share of the estate, wastes it in a far country and ends up feeding pigs. He comes back to himself and heads home to ask to be made a hired worker. His father sees him far off, runs, embraces him, cuts off his speech, dresses him in the best robe and throws a feast: "This son of mine was dead, and he has come back to life" (15:11–24). The elder son, coming in from the field, refuses to join the party and complains that he has slaved for years without so much as a goat. The father goes out to him too: "My child, you are with me all the time." The story ends without telling us whether he goes in (15:25–32).
readings: Read as God's welcome to sinners

The traditional reading: the shepherd, the woman and the father picture God, who seeks the lost and rejoices when they return; the younger son is the repentant sinner, and the elder son the self-righteous. This reading follows Luke's own frame (15:1–2) and refrains (15:7, 10).
Read through village eyes

Kenneth Bailey, after decades in Middle Eastern villages, read the father's actions as shocking: giving away property early, running in public, embracing a disgraced son before the village could shame him. The father takes the son's shame on himself, a picture of costly love, and the elder son's public refusal is a second rebellion as serious as the first.
Read as a Jewish story of losing and finding

Amy-Jill Levine argues that the stories are first about losing and finding, and about counting: a man with a hundred sheep, a woman with ten coins, a man with two sons, who must go out to the one he forgot. Read this way, the parable does not set Pharisees against sinners but asks every listener whether anyone in their own house is missing.

views.H: A hundred sheep was a medium-sized flock; ten drachmas, a poor household's savings. Inheritance law gave the elder of two sons a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), so the younger son's portion was a third. A "faraway country" with pig farms means Gentile land, perhaps the Greek cities of the Decapolis or beyond. Carob pods were animal feed. A fattened calf fed a village, and the robe, ring and sandals marked an honored son.
views.C: The lost sheep has a parallel in Matthew 18:12–14 and in the Gospel of Thomas 107 (where the lost sheep is the largest, loved "more than the ninety-nine"); the coin and the two sons are found only in Luke. Most scholars think Luke combined the sheep from a shared source (Q) with two stories from his own material (L) and supplied the frame of 15:1–2. The two sons is widely held to go back to Jesus, though some see Luke's hand in its polish and its refrain.
views.L: The chapter is one parable in three panels (15:3). Each moves from loss to search to finding to a call to rejoice, and the numbers narrow from a hundred to ten to two. The third breaks the pattern: the son "comes back to himself" while the father waits, and a second son appears who is lost at home. The refrain "was dead ... alive ... was lost ... found" (15:24, 32) and the unfinished ending turn the story back on the grumblers of 15:2.
views.J: The image of God as a shepherd seeking the lost comes from Ezekiel 34 and Psalm 23. Jewish teaching on repentance (teshuvah) held that God runs to meet the one who returns; a later rabbinic parable (Pesikta Rabbati 44:9) has a king tell his estranged son, "Return as far as you can, and I will come the rest of the way to you." Jewish readers have pointed out that the elder son is not condemned, only invited, and that reading him as "the Jews" turns a family story into a weapon.
views.T: The parable has been called "the gospel within the Gospel." Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic churches read it on the Sunday of the Prodigal Son, in the weeks of preparation before Great Lent, as a call to repentance. Western art has painted it often, above all Rembrandt's Return of the Prodigal Son (about 1668), which Henri Nouwen made the basis of a much-read book (1992). The shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders is among the oldest images of Christ in the catacombs.

deep.h: How to read the parable of the two sons
deep.b:
Readers have found at least four different centers in this story.

The repentant sinner. The classic preaching of the parable follows the younger son from rebellion through ruin to repentance and welcome. It is the story behind countless conversion testimonies and hymns.

The father. Many now call it the parable of the waiting or running father, since he is the only character in every scene and goes out to both sons. Kenneth Bailey argued that the father's public humiliation for the sake of his sons is the heart of the story.

The elder son. The frame of 15:1–2 suggests that the story is aimed at the grumblers, and its last scene, left open, invites them to come in. Joachim Jeremias called it the parable of the father's love, but stressed that it was spoken to critics of Jesus' table fellowship.

Jews and Gentiles. Some church fathers read the elder son as Israel and the younger as the Gentiles who came to faith; Jerome discusses this reading in his Letter 21. Modern scholars mostly set it aside, and Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine show how it fed contempt for Jews. Luke's own frame concerns Pharisees and sinners, all within Israel.

Some liberal Protestant thinkers around 1900, such as Adolf von Harnack in What Is Christianity?, treated this parable as the purest form of Jesus' message: a Father who forgives the returning son freely, with no sacrifice and no mediator. If so, they argued, the later church's doctrine of the atonement adds something Jesus did not teach.

Others reply that a parable makes its point without saying everything, and that Luke places it on the road to Jerusalem, where Jesus will die (9:51; 18:31–33). Kenneth Bailey argued that the father's run, embrace and public shame are themselves a picture of costly, self-giving love, the love the cross shows. Both sides agree on the central point: the father's welcome comes before the son can earn it.

echoes: Ezekiel 34:11–16; Psalm 23:1–4; Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 31:20; Hosea 11:1–9; Genesis 33:4; Genesis 41:42; Deuteronomy 21:17; Exodus 10:16; Leviticus 11:7; Jonah 4:1–11; Matthew 18:12–14; Matthew 21:28–32; 5:29–32; 7:34; 19:1–10

settings.what: The three parables of the lost (one parable in three panels)
settings.to: the Pharisees and scribes who were grumbling, with the tax collectors and sinners crowding around to listen
settings.when: on the journey to Jerusalem, when it had become known that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them
settings.why: To answer a single complaint, that he "takes sinners in, and eats with them." The stories defend his meals by showing them as God's own search and celebration, and invite the critics to join the joy instead of standing outside.
settings.readers: Luke's churches, where people from respectable backgrounds and people with a pagan or disreputable past shared one table, heard both a welcome and a warning against resentment.

settings.what: The parable of the lost sheep
settings.to: the grumbling Pharisees and scribes, in the hearing of tax collectors and sinners
settings.when: in answer to the complaint of 15:2
settings.why: To show that seeking one lost member of the flock is what any shepherd would do, and that heaven rejoices more over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who need no repentance. The listeners are asked to see themselves as the shepherd, not as the ninety-nine.
views: Told to critics, about sinners Jesus welcomes; the sheep is "lost" and the point is joy at its finding.
In Matthew 18:12–14 the same story is told to the disciples, about "these little ones" in the community who "stray"; the point is the leaders' duty not to let one be lost.

settings.what: The parable of the lost coin
settings.to: the same hearers
settings.when: following the lost sheep
settings.why: A twin to the first story, with a poor woman in place of a shepherd, so that both men's and women's work picture God's search. The careful sweeping and the call to her women neighbors stress the effort and the shared joy.

settings.what: The parable of the father and his two sons
settings.to: the Pharisees and scribes of 15:2, with tax collectors and sinners listening
settings.when: after the lost sheep and coin
settings.why: The younger son shows the sinners Jesus welcomes: lost, coming back, embraced before he can earn it. The elder son shows the grumblers: faithful, angry and outside. The father goes out to both. Because the story ends before the elder son answers, the listeners must decide whether to join the feast.
settings.readers: For Luke's churches the two sons could also be two kinds of believers, those raised in God's ways and those converted from far away, called to eat at one table (Acts 11:1–18; 15:1–29).
views: Most interpreters, following the frame, think the elder son is the point: the story asks Jesus' critics to share God's joy.
Christian preaching has often centered on the younger son as a call to repentance and an assurance of welcome.
Amy-Jill Levine reads it first as a story about a father who must go out to the son he had overlooked.

title: Money and the Great Gulf
sum: Jesus tells his disciples about a rich man's manager, accused of wasting his master's property and about to be fired. Too weak to dig and ashamed to beg, he calls in his master's debtors and has each write a smaller bill, so that they will take him into their homes. The master praises him for acting shrewdly. Jesus draws the lesson: use dishonest wealth to make friends who will welcome you into the everlasting tents; be faithful with little, and you will be trusted with much; you cannot be a slave both to God and to wealth (16:1–13).

The Pharisees, "fond of money," sneer. Jesus tells them that God knows their hearts, that the Law and the Prophets lasted until John and now the kingdom is being announced, that not a stroke of the Law will fall, and that divorce and remarriage is adultery (16:14–18). Then he tells of a rich man who feasted every day while a poor man named Lazarus lay at his gate covered in sores. Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's embrace; the rich man, in torment in Hades, begs for a drop of water and then for a messenger to warn his five brothers. Abraham answers: they have Moses and the Prophets, and if they will not listen to them, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead (16:19–31).
readings: Read as a chapter about money

Both parables begin with the same words, "a rich man" (16:1, 19), and the sayings between them are about wealth, faithfulness and the Pharisees' love of money. Read this way, the manager shows how to use money for the future, and the rich man shows what happens to someone who does not.
Read as a picture of the afterlife

Many readers have taken the second parable as a window on what happens after death: angels, Abraham's embrace, Hades, a fixed gulf. Others think Jesus used pictures his hearers already knew to make a point about this life, not to map the next. The card below gives the churches' views.
Read as a warning about hearing

The chapter ends with Moses, the Prophets and someone rising from the dead. Read this way, its last word is about Scripture: the Law and Prophets that still stand (16:17) already say how to treat the poor, and a heart that will not hear them will not be moved even by a resurrection.

views.H: Large estates in Galilee and Judea were often owned by absentee landlords and run by managers who leased land and collected rent in kind: oil and wheat, as in the bills of 16:6–7. Lending at interest to fellow Jews was forbidden by the Law but went on in disguised forms. Purple dye and fine linen were luxury goods of the very rich. Beggars, many of them disabled, gathered at the gates of the wealthy, and street dogs scavenged in every town.
views.C: The two parables are found only in Luke. Scholars disagree where the first ends (16:7, 8a, 8b or 9) and think 16:9–13 gathers sayings about money from different settings; 16:13 matches Matthew 6:24, and 16:16–18 has parallels scattered through Matthew (11:12–13; 5:18; 5:32). The rich man and Lazarus resembles an Egyptian tale and a Jewish story (see below), and some scholars think its second half (16:27–31) was added to an older folk tale, perhaps by Jesus himself.
views.L: The chapter is framed by two rich men (16:1, 19) and two kinds of welcome: the manager wants debtors to "take me into their own homes" (16:4), and Jesus speaks of being taken "into the everlasting tents" (16:9), which Lazarus receives and the rich man does not. The rich man "made merry" with the verb of the father's feast in 15:23–32. Reversal shapes the second parable: good things and bad, here and there, comfort and pain (16:25), as in Mary's song and the blessings and woes (1:52–53; 6:20–26).
views.J: Jesus sends the rich man's brothers to "Moses and the Prophets," the Jewish Scriptures, as enough to show the way of life. Jewish law commanded open-handed care for the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and later Jewish writings told stories of rich and poor reversed after death. Luke's portrait of the Pharisees as "fond of money" (16:14) is polemic; Josephus describes them as living simply, and Jewish scholars ask readers not to treat Luke's line as a fair account of the whole movement.
views.T: "Dives and Lazarus" became a favorite subject of medieval preaching, carving and song, and the funeral antiphon "In paradisum" prays that the dead may rest "with Lazarus, who once was poor." John Wesley's sermon on 16:9, "The Use of Money" (1760), shaped Methodist teaching on earning, saving and giving. The chapter has been central in Christian debates about the state of the dead, purgatory and prayer for the dead (see the card below).

deep.h: Four ways to read the shrewd manager
deep.b:
This may be the hardest of Jesus' parables. A dishonest manager is praised; how can that be?

1. Shrewdness, not honesty. The manager cheats his master again, and the point is only that he acted decisively when his future was at stake. Jesus says nothing in his favor except that he was shrewd (16:8), and calls him "crooked." The disciples should act with the same urgency for the kingdom.

2. He gave up his own cut. Joseph Fitzmyer, building on earlier work, argued that the reductions were the manager's own commission, added to the bills. By cutting it he lost his own profit, not his master's, and the master could admire him without being cheated.

3. He removed hidden interest. J. Duncan M. Derrett argued that the bills included interest forbidden by the Law (Deuteronomy 23:19), disguised as goods. Removing it made the master look righteous before God and the village, and he could not object without admitting that he had broken the Law. The larger cut on oil (half) than on wheat (a fifth) matches the higher rates charged for oil.

4. He gambled on his master's goodness. Kenneth Bailey argued that the debtors assumed the generous master had ordered the reductions, so the village praised him; to reverse them would cost the master honor. The manager, who had already seen his master's mercy in not jailing him, staked everything on it, as sinners must stake everything on God's mercy.

Each reading has defenders. John Kloppenborg has argued that the story's first hearers would have been surprised that the master praised a manager who had shamed him.

deep.h: The rich man and Lazarus and its parallels
deep.b:
Stories of a rich man and a poor man whose fates are reversed after death were told around the Mediterranean.

An Egyptian tale. A Demotic story written on a papyrus of the Roman period, known as Setne Khamwas and Si-Osire (or Setne II), tells how a father and his wonder-child watch two funerals: a rich man's, with great honor, and a poor man's, wrapped in a mat. The boy takes his father to the underworld, where the poor man stands near Osiris dressed in the rich man's fine linen, while the rich man suffers torment. Hugo Gressmann argued in 1918 that Jesus' parable came from this story through Jewish channels.

A Jewish story. The Jerusalem Talmud (Hagigah 2:2; Sanhedrin 6:9) tells of a rich tax collector, Bar Ma'yan, who received a grand funeral, and a poor Torah scholar who was buried with no one to mourn. In a dream a friend sees the scholar in a garden of springs, and the tax collector at the edge of a river, trying to reach the water with his tongue and unable to.

A Greek satire. Lucian's Downward Journey (2nd century AD) has a poor cobbler, Micyllus, and a rich tyrant reversed in the underworld; Ronald Hock has shown how Greek readers would have heard the parable against such stories.

Richard Bauckham's study of these parallels concludes that Jesus used a familiar pattern but turned its usual ending around. In many such tales a messenger returns from the dead to tell the living what awaits them. In Jesus' parable that request is refused: Moses and the Prophets are enough.

deep.h: Parable or account of real events?
deep.b:
Luke does not call the story a parable, and it is the only story of Jesus in which an invented character is given a name (Abraham, the other named figure, is the patriarch). Some Christian readers, from Tertullian (who used it to argue that the soul has a kind of body, On the Soul 7) to many modern evangelical preachers, have taken it as a true account of two men, or at least as a literal description of the afterlife.

Most scholars read it as a parable. It opens like other parables in Luke, "A certain man" (10:30; 14:16; 15:11; 16:1); it uses pictures common in Jewish and Greek stories of the time; and its details, such as a conversation across the gulf and a tongue that a drop of water would cool, are not meant to be mapped. Lazarus is named because his name means "God has helped" and because the closing lines turn on someone rising from the dead. On this view the parable tells us that how we treat the poor matters forever and that the choices of this life are decisive, without giving a diagram of the next. Christians who hold that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, such as Seventh-day Adventists and, in earlier centuries, Christian mortalists such as John Milton, read it this way. Others hold that, parable or not, Jesus would not build a story on a false picture of the afterlife.

echoes: Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Proverbs 16:5; Proverbs 31:20–22; 1 Samuel 16:7; Isaiah 58:6–7; Amos 6:4–7; Ezekiel 45:11–14; 1 Enoch 22:9–13; 1 Enoch 63:10; Matthew 6:24; Matthew 11:12–13; Matthew 5:18; Matthew 5:32; Mark 10:11–12; John 11:1–44; John 12:10; 1:52–53; 6:20–26; 12:13–21; 24:27, 44

settings.what: The parable of the shrewd manager
settings.to: his disciples, with the Pharisees listening (16:14)
settings.when: on the road to Jerusalem, right after the parables of the lost told to the Pharisees
settings.why: To teach disciples urgency and good sense about the future: a crooked man facing ruin acted at once to secure a place for himself, and "the children of light" should act at least as wisely with what is entrusted to them. It shocks on purpose, to make the point stick.
settings.readers: Luke's readers included believers with property and managers of others' property, who needed to know what money was for in a community that shared with the poor (Acts 4:32–37).
views: The parable praises only decisive action in a crisis, not dishonesty.
Several readings (commission, interest, Bailey's) make the manager's cancelled debts a picture of generosity that wins friends.

settings.what: Sayings about using wealth
settings.to: his disciples
settings.when: as the lesson of the manager's story
settings.why: To turn the parable into instruction: use money to make friends, especially the poor who can welcome you in the age to come; be faithful with money, which is small and not truly yours, so that God can trust you with true riches; and refuse to serve wealth as a master.
settings.readers: Luke's churches practiced giving to the poor as a central duty (Acts 2:45; 9:36; 10:2, 31), and these sayings gave it its reason.

settings.what: Words to the Pharisees about self-justification, the Law and divorce
settings.to: the Pharisees, who had been listening and sneering
settings.when: after the sayings on money
settings.why: To answer the sneer: God judges hearts, not reputations. The age of the Law and the Prophets has opened into the announcement of the kingdom, yet the Law still stands, and Jesus' teaching on divorce shows it made stricter, not looser. In Jewish law a husband could divorce his wife with a written document (Deuteronomy 24:1–4), and the schools debated the grounds; the saying binds husbands, and forbids remarriage after divorce as adultery.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers it showed that following Jesus did not mean throwing out the Law of Moses, a charge leveled at the early believers (Acts 6:13–14; 21:21).

settings.what: The parable of the rich man and Lazarus
settings.to: the Pharisees who loved money (16:14), with the disciples present
settings.when: after his words to the Pharisees about the Law
settings.why: To show where a life of ignoring the poor at one's gate ends, and that Moses and the Prophets already make God's will clear. The rich man's request for a messenger from the dead is refused: those who will not hear Scripture will not be convinced by a miracle.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew that Jesus had risen from the dead and that many still did not believe. The parable told rich believers to see the Lazarus at their own gate, and poor believers that God had not forgotten them.
views: Most scholars read it as a parable using familiar pictures, to teach about this life.
Many Christians through history have read its picture of Hades and Abraham's embrace as teaching about the state of the dead.

traditions.q: In the parable, the rich man is in torment in Hades and Lazarus is with Abraham, separated by a fixed gulf, before the judgment (16:22–26). What does it teach about the dead before the resurrection, and can anything change after death?
views: At death each soul receives its particular judgment, entering heaven (directly or after purification in purgatory) or hell (Catechism 1021–1022, 1030–1031). The Catechism cites this parable for the particular judgment and for the place where the righteous dead before Christ awaited him, "Abraham's bosom" (Catechism 633, 1021). The gulf separates the saved from the lost; purgatory concerns the saved and does not cross it.

The souls of the dead have a foretaste of joy or sorrow until the final judgment and the resurrection (Confession of Dositheus, decree 18). The Church prays for the departed, and the gulf is read as the separation of the righteous and the unrepentant, not as a bar to the Church's prayers.

Lutheran teachers cite the parable to show that souls are conscious after death and that a person's state is fixed at death, with no purgatory; the Smalcald Articles reject purgatory and Masses for the dead.

At death the souls of the righteous are received into heaven and those of the wicked are cast into hell, and "besides these two places, for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none" (Westminster Confession 32.1, which lists this parable among its proof texts).
The same as the Reformed view: believers' souls go at once to be with Christ, the wicked to torment, and there is no change of state after death (Second London Confession 31.1).

Evangelicals are divided. Most hold the Reformed and Baptist view. A minority hold conditional immortality: Edward Fudge argues that the parable describes Hades before the judgment, not the final punishment, so it does not show that the lost suffer forever, and John Stott tentatively favored the view that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished forever (Essentials, 1988).

The dead are unconscious until the resurrection (Fundamental Belief 26). The story is a parable using popular Jewish beliefs to teach how the choices of this life decide one's destiny; it is not a picture of what happens at death.

The account is a parable, not a literal description; the rich man stands for the religious leaders and Lazarus for the common people who accepted Jesus, and the change in their positions came with Jesus' ministry and its aftermath. The dead are conscious of nothing.

title: Faith, Thanks and the Coming Day
sum: Jesus warns his disciples that snares will come, but woe to the one who sets them; better a millstone around the neck than to trip up one of these little ones. If a brother sins, rebuke him; if he repents, forgive him, even seven times in one day. The apostles ask, "Give us more faith!" Jesus answers that faith the size of a mustard seed could uproot a mulberry tree and plant it in the sea. Then he tells of a slave who comes in from the field and is expected to serve supper first: so disciples who have done all they were told should say, "We are useless slaves. What we were bound to do, we have done" (17:1–10).

On the way to Jerusalem, between Samaria and Galilee, ten men with skin disease call out for mercy. Jesus sends them to show themselves to the priests, and on the way they are made clean. Only one comes back to thank him, and he is a Samaritan: "Your faith has saved you" (17:11–19). Asked by Pharisees when the kingdom of God is coming, Jesus says it does not come in a way that can be watched for: "the kingdom of God is among you." To the disciples he speaks of the day of the Son of Man, sudden as lightning, coming on people busy with ordinary life as in the days of Noah and Lot. On that day do not turn back; remember Lot's wife. One will be taken along and the other left behind. "Where, Lord?" they ask, and he answers with a proverb about vultures gathering where the body is (17:20–37).
readings: Read as instructions for the community

The first half of the chapter is about life together: not causing others to fall, rebuking and forgiving, trusting God, and serving without claiming credit. Read this way, it is a short rule for disciples who will live together after Jesus is gone.
Read as a story about gratitude and outsiders

The healing of the ten sets a Samaritan, the "foreigner," against nine who never come back. Read this way, the center of the chapter is the one who sees, turns back and gives thanks, and the outsider who becomes the model of faith.
Read as teaching about the end

The last section answers two questions: when the kingdom comes and what the day of the Son of Man will be like. Read this way, the chapter teaches both a kingdom already present in Jesus (17:21) and a day still to come (17:24), and calls disciples to live ready, without chasing rumors or clinging to possessions.

views.H: People with skin disease lived outside villages and depended on charity; a mixed group of Jews and a Samaritan is plausible in a border area. The priests' inspection followed Leviticus 13–14. The Pharisees' question reflects a time of intense expectation that God would act against Rome; the decades before AD 70 saw prophets and would-be messiahs who drew crowds into the wilderness, as Josephus describes.
views.C: 17:1–6 gathers sayings that Matthew places in his discourse on the church (Matthew 18:6–7, 15, 21–22) and elsewhere (Matthew 17:20). The slave's duty (17:7–10), the ten men (17:11–19) and the question about the kingdom (17:20–21) are Luke's alone. 17:22–37 shares material with Matthew 24 (Q, on the usual view), but Luke keeps it separate from his own discourse on Jerusalem's fall (21:5–36), so that the day of the Son of Man comes without warning signs.
views.L: Luke links scenes by words: "faith" (17:5–6, 19), "turn back" (17:4, 15, 18, 31), "see" (17:14, 15, 22). The ten men's story picks up Naaman (4:27) and the Samaritan of 10:33, and prepares for the mission to Samaria in Acts 8. The discourse on the day of the Son of Man is built on pairs: Noah and Lot, two in a bed, two at the mill, roof and field.
views.J: The healing sends the men to the priests, in obedience to the Law (Leviticus 14). The Pharisees' question about when the kingdom would come is a natural Jewish question, grounded in Daniel and the prophets. Noah and Lot were standard Jewish examples of judgment and rescue, paired in Wisdom of Solomon 10 as in 2 Peter 2. Jewish readers note that the Samaritan is called a "foreigner," the temple's word for those excluded, which shows how deep the division was.
views.T: The healing of the ten lepers is read in many churches as a lesson in thanksgiving; in the United States it is often read on Thanksgiving Day. "We are useless slaves" became a key text in the Reformation debates over merit (see the card below). "The kingdom of God is within you" (KJV) shaped Christian mysticism and inspired Tolstoy's book of that name. The "taken and left" sayings are central texts for belief in the rapture.

deep.h: The day of the Son of Man in Luke 17 and Luke 21
deep.b:
Luke has two discourses about the future. In chapter 21, in the temple, Jesus speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies and destroyed, with signs and warnings (21:5–36). In chapter 17, on the road, he speaks of the day of the Son of Man, which comes without warning, like lightning, like the flood, like the fire on Sodom. Matthew and Mark combine the two kinds of material in one discourse (Matthew 24; Mark 13).

Readers have explained Luke's arrangement in different ways. Many think Luke separated the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, already past when he wrote, from the return of Christ, still future, so that readers would not tie Christ's coming to the city's fall. Preterist readers, who see much of Jesus' prophecy fulfilled in AD 70, take some of chapter 17 that way too. Futurist readers see the sudden day of 17:24–37 as the second coming, and many Dispensationalists see the "taken" of 17:34–35 as the rapture. Most agree that Luke insists on two things at once: the kingdom is already present in Jesus (17:21), and its full coming is still ahead (17:24).

settings.what: Sayings on snares and forgiveness
settings.to: his disciples
settings.when: on the road, after the parable of the rich man and Lazarus
settings.why: To warn disciples against leading weaker believers into sin, and to make rebuke and forgiveness the normal life of the community: correct a brother who sins, and forgive him whenever he repents, without limit.
settings.readers: Luke's churches faced the strains of a mixed community, with disputes over the Law, food and money (Acts 6:1; 15:1–2); this was its rule for handling wrongs.

settings.what: The apostles' request for faith, and Jesus' answer
settings.to: Jesus; then Jesus to the apostles
settings.when: after the command to forgive without limit
settings.why: The apostles feel unequal to such forgiveness and ask for more faith. Jesus answers that the amount is not the issue: even the smallest real trust in God can do what looks impossible.

settings.what: The parable of the slave's duty
settings.to: the apostles
settings.when: continuing his answer about faith
settings.why: To keep disciples from thinking that faith and obedience give them a claim on God. A slave who has done his work has done no more than he owed; disciples who have done all God commands should say the same. It corrects pride, especially in those who will lead the church.
settings.readers: For leaders of Luke's churches, the apostles' successors, it ruled out treating ministry as a ground for honor or reward (compare 22:24–27; Acts 20:33–35).

settings.what: Jesus' words to ten men with skin disease and to the Samaritan who returned
settings.to: ten men with skin disease outside a village between Samaria and Galilee, then the one Samaritan who came back
settings.when: on the way to Jerusalem
settings.why: The order to show themselves to the priests followed the Law of Leviticus 14, which required a person cleansed of skin disease to be examined and declared clean by a priest, so that he could return to his family and the community; it bound the healed person and the priests. Jesus' later questions expose the nine who did not return, and his words to the Samaritan, "Your faith has saved you," show that thanks and faith had brought this foreigner more than a cure.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw the Samaritans and other outsiders who would receive the good news (Acts 1:8; 8:4–25), and a model of grateful faith.

settings.what: The answer about when the kingdom comes
settings.to: Pharisees who asked when the kingdom of God was coming
settings.when: on the journey to Jerusalem
settings.why: To turn the question away from calculating dates and watching for signs, and to point to the kingdom already present in Jesus' own words and acts. The Pharisees, who were watching Jesus closely, are told that the kingdom is right among them.
views: Most modern scholars: the kingdom is present in Jesus and his work.
Many church fathers and the KJV: the kingdom is an inner, spiritual reality.
A minority: it is within their grasp, if they will accept it.

settings.what: The discourse on the day of the Son of Man
settings.to: his disciples
settings.when: after the Pharisees' question about the kingdom
settings.why: To prepare the disciples for a time when Jesus would be absent and they would long for his presence: not to follow false alarms, to know that the Son of Man must suffer first, and to live ready for a day that will come suddenly on people absorbed in ordinary life, when they must not turn back for their possessions.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, living after Jesus' death and resurrection (and, on the usual dating, after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70), and still waiting for his return, were taught to live watchful and detached, without fixing dates.
views: Most Christians read 17:22–37 of the second coming.
Preterist readers take part or all of it as fulfilled in the Roman war.

traditions.q: "When you have done all you were ordered to do, say, 'We are useless slaves. What we were bound to do, we have done'" (17:10). Can Christians merit anything before God, and can anyone do more than God requires ("works of supererogation")?
views: The good works of the justified, done in grace, truly merit an increase of grace and eternal life, yet this merit is itself God's gift: in crowning our merits God crowns his own gifts (Council of Trent, session 6, canon 32; Catechism 2006–2011). Beyond the commandments Christ gave counsels of perfection, such as poverty and celibacy, and the merits of Christ and the saints form a treasury on which the Church draws in granting indulgences (Catechism 1476–1477). Catholic teachers read 17:10 as forbidding pride, not as denying merit.

Good works done in faith are not mere signs of faith but its fruits, through which faith becomes effective, and God rewards them according to his promises (Confession of Dositheus, decree 13). Orthodox teachers do not use the Latin categories of a treasury of merits or of works of supererogation; they speak of synergy, a person's cooperation with God's grace, rather than of a reckoning of merit.

No one can do more than God's law requires, or even fulfil it; good works follow faith but earn nothing before God. Melanchthon's Apology of the Augsburg Confession answers the opponents' use of Christ's words, that having done all we are unprofitable servants, in its article on love and the fulfilling of the law (Article IV, numbered V in some editions), and rejects works of supererogation in its articles on repentance and satisfactions (XII) and on monastic vows (XXVII).

"We cannot by our best works merit pardon of sin, or eternal life at the hand of God," since "when we have done all we can, we have done but our duty, and are unprofitable servants" (Westminster Confession 16.5, quoting this verse). No one can do more than God requires (16.4).

Article 14 of the Thirty-Nine Articles, "Of Works of Supererogation," calls such works impossible and arrogant, citing this verse: "When ye have done all that are commanded to you, say, We are unprofitable servants."

John Wesley kept the same article in the Articles of Religion he sent to American Methodists (Article 11), while also teaching that believers can grow toward Christian perfection in love, which is God's work in them, not a surplus of merit.
